messages.subject: bootstrap options in model definition
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have made a density and abundance estimate for cetacean species in
two strata. I assumed f(0) was the same for both and modelled it
pooled over strata. Density was estimated per stratum.

I want to make a bootstrap estimate of variace for D, but am not sure
which option to chose in the model defiinition of DISTANCE i.e.
should I resample samples within strata or resample observations
within samples?

I have 7 samples in stratum A and 9 samples in stratum B (each sample
respresented by total effort over a day to maintain independence
between samples), so I am concerned that the sample sizes are too
small to consider for bootstrapping.

Any advice as to which method is most appropriate  and perhaps an
explanation of the circumstances in which one option (observations or
samples) for botstrapping would be preferable, would be a great help.

I have the Distance book but can't seem to find anything to clarify
this.

Many thanks
Kelly

messages.subject: Re: bootstrap options in model definition
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kelly, List:

Here's my thoughts - perhaps others have different opinions.

You're right that you have few samples for bootstrapping.  Indeed you have few
for making a robust empirical estimate of variance in encounter rate.  Ideally
you want 15-20 per stratum as a minimum.  Above that, the more the better.  You
can give it a go, but you should be aware that your results are likely to be
unreliable.

As for which of the bootstrapping options is most appropriate, you can work
this out by considering how your experiment was set up:

Normally, we assign our study area to strata, and then randomly (maybe
systematic randomly) assign our sample locations within strata.  So strata are
fixed and samples are random.  In bootstrapping, you try to re-create the
process that lead to the data being collected.  Therefore, you want to resample
samples within strata (ie choose a new set of samples in each bootstrap
replicate, but leave the strata fixed).

Rarely, the strata are also random.  For example, you may be intersted in mean
density in your study area over a one-month period, and have picked a random
subset of 15 days, surveying different transects in the whole study area each
day.  In this case, you would resample strata and samples within strata.

I can't think of a case when you'd want to resample observations within
samples.  The option is only there for completeness.  Has anyone out there ever
used it?

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.subject: Pooling random subsets
messages.body_plain:
Dear list;

We have a large data set (>6000)  of line transect data
collected over many years in several areas. In any one year
we usually obtain between 20 to 80 contacts (distances).
Thus, we usually end up with either pooling data in one area
over years or neighbouring areas in any one year.

We believe it would be reasonable to assume that the
detection function would be the same although the ESW
could vary between areas and year. We have pooled the
original data in different subsets (year or area to obtain
between 70 and 400 observations), and find that Neg. Exp.
("poorly collected data") is selected most of the time
according to AIC.  Hazard is chosen as the next best. There
is a small difference in AIC but substantial difference in
ESW.

I therefore took randomly selected subsets of all the
observations by adding a random variable and sorting the
data set on that variable. I then copied  the first 35, 75,
125, 250 or 500 observations from the large data set, 30
times for each of the 5 groups. The pattern that develops is
that no clear winner can be seen at 35 observations, neg exp
is chosen at 75 observations. But hazard comes out as clear
winner with neg exp as a clear second at the higher sample
sizes.

However, it doesn't appear to be any relationship between
sample size and function chosen in the pooling of original
strata above. Also pooling all the original data (detection
by all) into one sample still gives neg exp.

Is this due to that I pick all the observations in one
subset without replacement, e.g. the first 35 observations
in a randomly sorted file? The results from the
randomization shows a rather interesting pattern with sample
size and esw depending on chosen function otherwise, but
since my statistical training is poor I feel the need for
some advice!

All the best;

Tomas Willebrand

Recently I posted a query regarding = estimating the=20 probability of detection for distances <w.  Below I provide a = summary of=20 my results based on suggestions from others and my own=20 investigation.
 
In my original email I didn't clearly = explain that=20 what I wanted was the probability of detection for distances <w = (i.e., the=20 area under the detection curve for some distance x, where = x<w),=20 not just the detection probability at distance x.
 
Why would one want to do this?  In = my case,=20 many people survey grassland birds using strip transects and assume the=20 probability of detection is 1.0.  And the strip widths used vary=20 greatly.  I wanted to use my data to estimate probabilities of = detection at=20 various strip widths.
 
It is possible to obtain the = probability of=20 detection for x<w, as well as a 95% CI, using Distance, but = only=20 for simple detection functions.  First, you analyze your data = and=20 select the best model (it can only be a half-normal with no adjustments = or a=20 uniform with a 2nd-order adjustment).  Second, re-run the analysis = with the=20 bootstrap variance (and bootstrap output file) but only permit the model = you=20 selected to be estimated in all the bootstrap runs.
 
The third step gets more involved and = depends on=20 the model function.
 
1.  From the bootstrap output you = can obtain=20 f(0) and the transect width (w) for each resample.
2.  Using (1) you can obtain the = parameter=20 estimate for each resample.  For the uniform with a 2nd-order = adjustment=20 solve for A(1) from the following relationship:
          &nbs= p;        =20 f(0) =3D 1/[(1+A(1)/3)*w]
where w is the width for the = resample.
 
For the half-normal you have to = iteratively solve=20 the following equation
 
          &nbs= p;        =20 f(0) =3D 1/sqrt(2*pi)*A(1)*[PHI(w(i)/A(1)-.5)]  where=20 pi=3D3.14159265, PHI() is the = cdf for the=20 normal distribution, sqrt() is the square root, and w(i) is the width of = interest, i.e., w(i)<w.
 
3.  After solving for A(1) for = each resample=20 you can calculate the probability of detection over the interval 0 to = w(i) for=20 the uniform w/ 2nd-order adj as
 
       =20             =    =20 P(from 0 to w(i)) =3D (w(i)/w+A(1)/w**3/3*w(i)**3)/(w(i)/w)
 
and for the half-normal = as
 
           =20             P(from 0 to=20 w(i)) =3D(SQRT(2*pi)*A(1)*(PHI(w(i)/A(1))-0.5))/w(i)
 
Fourth, now that you have the probability of detection for each = resample,=20 simply select the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles to obtain a 95% CI (note: the = point=20 estimate is obtained by plugging in the coefficient values from the = Distance=20 output into (3)).
 
 
The reason you can only obtain these values for the simplest = uniform and=20 half-normal functions is that all other functions have >1 coefficient = (even=20 the simplest hazard function) and you end up with 1 equation with=20 >2 unknown coefficients.  What is needed are the = coefficients for=20 each resample run, but that is not currently available in the bootstrap = output=20 in Distance.  That way you would simply plug in the coefficients = and could=20 either analytically or iteratively estimate the area under the detection = function for the width of interest.
 
Another possibility is to integrate the model = function and then=20 use the delta method to estimate a variance and obtain CIs, but I = suspect the=20 bootstrap is still a much better approach, and my calculus is too rusty = to=20 integrate the hazard function (if it's even possible)!  If someone = out=20 there can integrate the hazard, please let me know!
 
Thanks to Jeff Laake and Steve Buckland for their help=20 and suggestions (but all the errors are my own!).
 
Duane
